title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery
authors: Samidha Verma, Ankit Anand, Sayan Ranu
abstract: Modern automated heuristic discovery (AHD) systems increasingly rival hand-crafted heuristics by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively mutate and refine solutions. A natural assumption is that more powerful and more expensive models consistently yield better heuristics. We challenge this empirically: across multiple NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, we find no consistent advantage for larger, costlier models. This raises a deeper question: given a pool of LLMs spanning frontier and freely hosted or open-weight models, how should one adaptively select which model to invoke at each step of the search? The challenge is non-trivial. The optimal LLM may shift over the course of a run, and because one LLM's output seeds the context for subsequent calls, each model's reward signal is non-stationary and entangled across the heuristic population, thus violating the independence assumptions of classical online decision-making settings. We address this through Ballad (Bandit-based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery), an online bandit algorithm that learns to orchestrate a pool of LLMs into an ensemble that matches or exceeds what any soloist LLM achieves alone. This orchestration is powered by an LLM selection policy that favors rare, high-scoring heuristics over stable averages, a DAG-based credit propagation mechanism through the genealogy of the heuristic population, and discounting of stale observations to remain attuned to each model's current utility. Across five NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems and a pool of four models of varying capability and cost, Ballad not only matches the best individual LLM in hindsight but, in several cases, surpasses every individual model while reducing API cost by up to 65.6% relative to always using the strongest model.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive LLM routing can match or outperform the best single model for automated heuristic discovery without always relying on the largest, costliest model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ballad offers a way to reduce API spending while maintaining or improving heuristic quality in combinatorial optimization workflows.
method: Use online bandit routing to select an LLM at each search step, favoring rare, high-scoring heuristics over stable averages.
Propagate credit through a DAG representing the heuristic population’s genealogy.
Discount stale observations to track each model’s changing utility.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five NP-hard optimization problems and four LLMs, Ballad matched the best individual model in hindsight, sometimes surpassed every individual model, and reduced API cost by up to 65.6% versus always using the strongest model.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover five problems and four models; performance and savings may differ with other model pools, pricing, or search budgets.
infographic.paper_title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery

title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
authors: Yihan Xia, Wenxin Xu, Taotao Wang
abstract: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

infographic.key_insight: Accelerating verifiable AI requires matching hardware and proof-system optimizations to workload-specific bottlenecks, rather than optimizing cryptographic kernels in isolation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers must assess memory capacity, instruction issue and synchronization alongside execution time and bandwidth when selecting hardware for zero-knowledge proving.
method: Link AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware through a four-layer framework.
Review the literature and measure six provers and seven kernels.
Analyze bottlenecks to guide hardware selection and proof-system optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measurements show shifting costs across proof systems and input lengths; a 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds 40 GB GPU capacity but completes on an 80 GB device.
infographic.watch_item: Kernel-level speedups may not translate into end-to-end gains when memory capacity or other proof-generation stages dominate.
infographic.paper_title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help

title: Your Vision Foundation Model Is Secretly an EEG Foundation Model
authors: Guoan Wang, Feng Liu
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are pretrained on thousands of hours of recordings, yet their frozen features transfer poorly to downstream tasks, and this transfer does not consistently improve with larger models or more pretraining data. We show that a vision foundation model that has never seen EEG is a stronger frozen EEG encoder than these specialized models, once the signals are rendered as images that a vision transformer can read. Our method, SeeEEG, keeps the vision backbone frozen and learns only how EEG is displayed to it. Each channel occupies a dedicated row of patches and is drawn either as a waveform at a fixed gain or as a scalogram whose frequency range spans the patch height, so that task-relevant patterns fall within individual tokens. The montage, filtering, and contrast parameters of this display are initialized from a standard clinical montage and optimized with the task loss through the frozen backbone, which amounts to at most 1,113 trainable parameters per view. We compare SeeEEG with seven EEG foundation models on eight clinical, sleep, affective, and brain-computer interface datasets, with every encoder frozen and paired with identical readout heads. With a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B, SeeEEG outperforms every EEG foundation model in balanced accuracy on all eight datasets and reaches a mean rank of 1.3 in Cohen kappa or AUROC, compared with 2.9 for the strongest baseline, REVE. The learned displays transfer without further optimization to the video encoder V-JEPA 2.1, which outperforms every EEG foundation model on both metrics on six of the eight datasets. Replacing DINOv3 with a randomly initialized ViT-B lowers the score by 15.2 points on average, so the ability to read rendered EEG comes from visual pretraining.

infographic.key_insight: A frozen vision foundation model can outperform specialized EEG foundation models when EEG signals are rendered as task-optimized images.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SeeEEG offers a parameter-efficient way to reuse pretrained vision encoders for EEG tasks by learning the signal display rather than updating the backbone.
method: Render each EEG channel in a dedicated patch row as a fixed-gain waveform or frequency-scaled scalogram.
Optimize montage, filtering, and contrast through the frozen backbone using at most 1,113 trainable parameters per view.
Evaluate frozen encoders with identical readout heads and transfer learned displays to V-JEPA 2.1 without further display optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight datasets, DINOv3-based SeeEEG beat seven EEG foundation models in balanced accuracy on every dataset; replacing DINOv3 with a random ViT-B reduced scores by 15.2 points on average.
infographic.watch_item: The results establish frozen-encoder performance, not superiority over fine-tuned EEG models, and display optimization still requires task supervision.
infographic.paper_title: Your Vision Foundation Model Is Secretly an EEG Foundation Model

title: Media Trading with Censored Auction Prices: A Stochastic Control and Reinforcement Learning Approach
authors: Yun-Ithry Gamrani, Huyên Pham
abstract: In real-time bidding, marketing agencies must balance campaign performance, transaction margins and the use of a finite advertising budget. A key difficulty is that market-clearing prices are typically observed only when bids are successful, so the information available for subsequent decisions depends on the bidding policy. We formulate this problem using a continuous-time stochastic control model with a latent price process. To construct a price signal, we consider parallel exploratory subcampaigns in which bids are randomized subject to an upper bound. Under a stylized cross-sectional sampling model, the resulting price estimator is consistent and satisfies a mean-square error bound of order $N^{-1}$, where $N$ is the number of exploratory observations. We then describe a model-based approach combining forward-equation calibration with Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman policy iteration and a physics-informed neural network, alongside an entropy-regularized actor-critic approach based on observable information in a model-free setting. Synthetic experiments illustrate the estimator and the computational procedures. The framework clarifies the decision and information trade-offs faced by the agency, while distinguishing full-information benchmarks and estimated-price policies from the genuinely partially observed control problem.

infographic.key_insight: Bidding determines both advertising outcomes and access to price information, making media trading a joint control-and-learning problem under censored auction prices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports bidding-system design that balances campaign performance, transaction margins, finite budgets, and price exploration.
method: Model bidding as continuous-time stochastic control with latent market prices.
Estimate prices using parallel exploratory subcampaigns with randomized, upper-bounded bids.
Compute policies via forward-equation calibration, HJB policy iteration and a physics-informed neural network, or observable-information entropy-regularized actor-critic learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic experiments illustrate estimation and computation; under a stylized cross-sectional sampling model, the price estimator is consistent with mean-square error of order N⁻¹.
infographic.watch_item: Full-information benchmarks and estimated-price policies do not resolve the genuinely partially observed problem, and real-world validation is not reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Media Trading with Censored Auction Prices: A Stochastic Control and Reinforcement Learning Approach

title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation
authors: Ethan Mollick, Lilach Mollick, Ben Przystanski, LJ Ciccarelli, Natalie Bach, Laura Zarrow
abstract: Educational simulations are a well-established pedagogical technique that gives learners opportunities to apply knowledge, respond to challenges, and reflect on their performance. High-quality simulations, however, are difficult to build, requiring instructor input, scenario design, character development, scaffolding, technical implementation, and repeated revision. This paper presents Primer, an open-source, LLM-agnostic AI-supported system that helps educators create adaptive educational simulations. Educators contribute their knowledge of the subject, lesson, and students, while generative AI produces responsive variations of practice for students. Primer uses a multi-agent system centered around executing educator's instructional intent through the entire learning experience. We hope that by releasing Primer as an open-source system, including its prompts and GitHub repository, we provide a foundation for development and research on educator-in-the-loop AI authoring, multi-agent educational workflows, and simulation-based pedagogy. Further, by allowing the use of various AI models, including local and open source models, we provide the opportunity for implementation under varied governance regimes. Primer points toward a model of educational AI in which instructors can create locally grounded practice opportunities based on their own materials, goals, examples, and knowledge of students.

infographic.key_insight: Primer is an open-source, LLM-agnostic framework that helps instructors create adaptive educational simulations grounded in their teaching goals and knowledge of students.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its multi-agent architecture supports educator-guided simulation authoring and model choice, including local and open-source models for varied governance requirements.
method: Instructors provide subject knowledge, lesson goals, materials, and student context.
A multi-agent system carries instructional intent through simulation creation and delivery.
Generative AI produces responsive variations of student practice.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the framework and release of prompts and a GitHub repository, but reports no quantitative evaluation or learning-outcome data.
infographic.watch_item: Faithfulness to instructional intent and educational effectiveness require validation before classroom deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation

title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
authors: Jiacheng Xu, Shuo He, Fuxiang Zhang, Chaojie Wang, Bo An
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically relies on a verifier that can reliably judge whether sampled solutions are correct. However, in many realistic settings, complete verification is generally unavailable, while cheap checks can only falsify failures. We formalize this regime as one-sided verifiability (OSV): verified negatives are reliable counterexamples, but verified positives are merely non-falsified candidates and may contain many false positives. This asymmetry makes standard RLVR unreliable, because reinforcing verified positives can directly reward shortcuts that pass partial checks. To address this issue, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), which treats verified positives as unlabeled and updates the policy only by suppressing trusted verified negatives. Specifically, NOPO combines a reference-relative negative suppression loss with a group-level adapter that scales each update by the proportion of non-falsified responses. Across unit-test, constraint-check, and LLM self-verifiers, NOPO improves pass@k over baselines on code, logic, and math benchmarks when oracle rewards are unavailable. These gains persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.

infographic.key_insight: When partial checks reliably identify failures but cannot confirm correctness, suppressing verified negatives avoids directly rewarding false positives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: NOPO offers a policy-training approach for settings where unit tests, constraint checks, or LLM verifiers can reject failures but cannot certify successful solutions.
method: Treat non-falsified responses as unlabeled rather than correct.
Apply a reference-relative loss to suppress trusted verified negatives.
Scale each update by the group’s proportion of non-falsified responses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved pass@k over baselines on code, logic, and math benchmarks, with gains persisting under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.
infographic.watch_item: NOPO assumes verified negatives are reliable; erroneous failure labels could suppress valid solutions.
infographic.paper_title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards

title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
authors: Qijia Zhuang, Yanyi Gou, Wenbin Ma, Yuxiang Ren
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps. We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively. We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

infographic.key_insight: Skill Adapter personalizes reusable agent skills and dynamically routes them as tasks, inputs, and environments change.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a way to adapt shared agent procedures to user-specific tools and requirements while managing growing skill libraries.
method: Distill user requirements and execution feedback into Adapters linked to general-purpose skills.
Route applicable skills and Adapters into an online task library, preloading candidates and rechecking them when inputs become available.
Use reinforcement learning to optimize modification and routing decisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench, Skill Adapter improves task success by an average of 11.43 percentage points over SkillRL, reduces mean execution time on all three, and retains its performance advantage with 1,000 skills.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify training costs or adapter-maintenance overhead, which matter for deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills

title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
authors: Tiago de Souza Farias, Caio Moraes Porto, Matheus da Silva Fonseca, Nicolas Armando Cabrera Carpi, Anderson de Araujo Oliveira, Celso Jorge Villas-Boas
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

infographic.key_insight: A frozen, general-purpose LLM can propose promising quantum-circuit parameters when Hamiltonians have identifiable structure, but performs worse than Adam on general random Hamiltonians.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLM-generated circuit parameters enable independently verifiable energy calculations, making them more trustworthy engineering outputs than direct energy predictions.
method: Generate complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions.
Optionally provide iterative energy feedback and compare performance with Adam optimization.
Evaluate random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, molecular systems, and blind circuit interpretation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations found larger energy errors than Adam for general Hamiltonians, limited gains from feedback, and promising low-energy configurations for structured Hamiltonians.
infographic.watch_item: Direct LLM energy predictions can violate spectral lower bounds, so independently evaluate generated circuit parameters rather than trusting predicted energies.
infographic.paper_title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models

title: Al-Ghasali: A Computational Framework for Simulating Islamic Jurisprudential Rulings via Finite State Automata and Large Language Models
authors: Elnaserledinellah Mahmoud Abdelwahab
abstract: This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim that extract minimal operational rules as simple Horn clause logical programs, this work proves that the semantics of closed Fiqh chapters collapse completely to deterministic Finite State Automata (FSA). We establish a formal computational hierarchy, demonstrating that restricting formalization to finite propositional Horn theories guarantees decidability and constant time (O(1)) verdict extraction after offline compilation. The framework formally proves that hierarchical compositions of sub-chapter FSAs preserve this O(1) complexity, and that temporal juristic requirements, such as Tartib (order), are deterministically flattened into static ontological states, preserving the memoryless property of the automaton. To generate human-readable juristic summaries, Al Ghasali incorporates Large Language Models (LLMs) via an architecture where the deterministic FSA strictly controls the probabilistic LLM. Crucially, the paper formulates sufficient design safety conditions for this FSA LLM integration, ensuring strict adherence to the epistemological boundaries of Usul al Fiqh. To neutralize the risk of LLM hallucination, the system employs a Grammar Guided Constrained Decoding mechanism. We formally define the mapping function that dynamically constructs unambiguous right linear grammars from the FSA execution history. The paper mathematically proves that this architecture, augmented by a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking, guarantees the absolute absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination, and Semantic Inversion reducing the LLM to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts

infographic.key_insight: Al-Ghasali models closed Islamic jurisprudential chapters as deterministic finite-state automata, using constrained LLMs only to verbalize computed rulings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a design for rule-governed AI systems that separate deterministic decisions from probabilistic language generation.
method: Compile finite propositional Horn rules into deterministic automata for O(1) verdict extraction.
Compose sub-chapter automata and encode ordering requirements in explicit states.
Constrain LLM output with execution-derived grammars, a bounded neutral lexicon, and valence locking.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports formal proofs of complexity preservation and conditional hallucination prevention, but provides no datasets, benchmarks, or empirical evaluation results.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees depend on correct and complete rule formalization and faithfully implemented decoding constraints; offline compilation costs and state-space growth require scrutiny.
infographic.paper_title: Al-Ghasali: A Computational Framework for Simulating Islamic Jurisprudential Rulings via Finite State Automata and Large Language Models

title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control
authors: Bowen Wang, Osvaldo Simeone
abstract: Online conformal risk control (OCRC) enables reliable uncertainty quantification in machine learning by converting model outputs into prediction sets with long-term risk guarantees. These guarantees, however, hinge on the assumption that the loss of each round is revealed immediately and losslessly. In practice, feedback may be delayed, and limited resources may prevent tracking all pending predictions, causing some feedback to be lost. To address this challenge, we develop capacity-aware OCRC (CA-OCRC), a framework that jointly determines how to allocate limited tracking feedback capacity and how to construct prediction sets. CA-OCRC is based on a randomized tracking policy that samples a proxy delay to decide whether, and for how long, feedback for the current round is tracked. CA-OCRC updates the prediction sets via inverse probability weighting, compensating for the possibility of feedback lost due to delays and limited tracking capacity. We analyze risk bounds for both arbitrary and stochastic delays, revealing a trade-off between receiving more feedback and avoiding capacity saturation. Building on these bounds, we optimize the proxy delay distribution, showing scaling laws for the tracking capacity that ensure the same long-term risk as OCRC with unlimited feedback. Experiments on medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications show the effectiveness of CA-OCRC as compared to existing OCRC mechanisms.

infographic.key_insight: Capacity-aware online conformal risk control (CA-OCRC) accounts for delayed and missing feedback while targeting long-term risk guarantees under limited tracking capacity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CA-OCRC supports uncertainty-aware prediction systems where feedback arrives late and only a limited number of pending predictions can be tracked.
method: Sample proxy delays to decide whether and how long to track each prediction.
Use inverse probability weighting to compensate for feedback lost through delays or capacity limits.
Optimize the proxy delay distribution using risk bounds for arbitrary and stochastic delays.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluations in medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications, showing effectiveness against existing OCRC methods without specifying numerical gains.
infographic.watch_item: Tracking-policy design must balance feedback collection against capacity saturation; matching unlimited-feedback long-term risk depends on sufficient capacity under the derived scaling laws.
infographic.paper_title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control

title: Support-Constrained Offline Policy Improvement for Pediatric ECMO from Limited Clinical Data
authors: Fateme Golivand Darvishvand, Saurabh Mathur, Nikhilesh Prabhakar, Michael A. Skinner, Ameet Soni, Neel Shah
abstract: Managing children on ECMO (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation) requires balancing short-term physiological stability with the long-term goal of preventing neurological injury. Standard reinforcement learning can propose risky, out-of-distribution actions, while imitation learning is limited to reproducing clinician behavior. We introduce Support-Constrained Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI-SC), an offline reinforcement learning framework that cautiously improves upon expert behavior by restricting optimization to empirically supported state-action pairs and defaulting to the clinician baseline in low-data regions. On 78 pediatric trajectories totaling over 6,000 hours of clinical data, we evaluate our framework using Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and a behavioral disagreement. Additionally, we formalize the performance-safety trade-off by introducing a unified Balance Score ($S(π)$). Our empirical evaluation shows that support-constrained policy improves the Balance Score by 38\% relative to FQI, improves estimated value by 1.28 FQE units over imitation learning, and reduces disagreement with clinician actions by 71\% relative to FQI.

infographic.key_insight: Support-constrained offline reinforcement learning improves estimated pediatric ECMO decision quality while staying closer to clinician behavior than standard Fitted Q-Iteration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Empirical support constraints and clinician fallback offer a practical design pattern for limiting out-of-distribution actions in data-scarce clinical decision systems.
method: Use Support-Constrained Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI-SC) to restrict optimization to empirically supported state-action pairs.
Default to the clinician baseline in low-data regions.
Evaluate estimated value with Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE), clinician-action disagreement, and a unified Balance Score.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 78 pediatric trajectories spanning over 6,000 clinical hours, FQI-SC improved Balance Score by 38% and reduced clinician-action disagreement by 71% versus FQI, while gaining 1.28 FQE units over imitation learning.
infographic.watch_item: Offline estimates and clinician agreement do not establish clinical safety or neurological benefit; prospective validation is needed before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Support-Constrained Offline Policy Improvement for Pediatric ECMO from Limited Clinical Data

title: Entire sig-jump-diffusions, their expected signature and applications to score-based generative modeling
authors: Christa Cuchiero, Francesca Primavera, Sara Svaluto-Ferro
abstract: We develop score-based generative models for time series and standard finite-dimensional data, building on the analytical computation of the expected signature of a new class of jump-diffusions, called entire sig-jump-diffusions. These are semimartingales whose characteristics are given by linear combinations of potentially infinitely many components of their own signature. We show that their expected signature can be computed by solving linear ODEs in the extended tensor algebra, providing a tractable foundation for learning procedures. Specifically, the learning of a generalized score function for jump diffusions, a key ingredient of our generative modeling framework, can be reduced to solving linear ODEs and a deterministic optimization problem. We further prove that polynomial jump-diffusions can be embedded into this framework, and that their expected signature reduces to a finite-dimensional system of linear ODEs. Building on this result, we develop an alternative approach for finite-dimensional data, based on inverse signature matching, a method that learns the score by matching the expected signature of the reverse process with that of the inverse forward signature.

infographic.key_insight: Entire sig-jump-diffusions make expected signatures computable through linear ODEs, enabling a tractable foundation for score-based generative modeling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a deterministic route to training jump-diffusion generators for time series and finite-dimensional data.
method: Define jump-diffusions whose characteristics are linear combinations of their own signature components.
Compute expected signatures via linear ODEs and learn generalized scores through deterministic optimization.
Embed polynomial jump-diffusions in finite-dimensional ODE systems and use inverse signature matching for finite-dimensional data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical results, including finite-dimensional closure for polynomial jump-diffusions, but no datasets, benchmarks, or empirical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: General models involve potentially infinite signature expansions, making practical truncation and computational scaling important implementation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Entire sig-jump-diffusions, their expected signature and applications to score-based generative modeling

title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Haochen Liu, Qianhao Zhu, Zixuan Wang, Dingming Li, Tongbo Chen, Peng Qiu
abstract: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

infographic.key_insight: A decision model that acts poorly can still teach effectively by judging actions after their consequences are visible.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Use retrospective action-level feedback to improve agent policies rather than selecting teachers solely by their own task success.
method: Compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld.
Judge complete trajectories by asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed.
Use JEV as a reinforcement-learning teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop.
infographic.evidence_signal: JEV teaching improved Qwen2.5-1.5B success over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop.
infographic.watch_item: Teacher results cover one teacher and two benchmarks; retrospective judging also requires completed trajectories.
infographic.paper_title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents

title: Designing Institutions for Autonomous AI
authors: Petter Törnberg
abstract: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions governing their interactions. Yet AI research has largely focused on individual agents. In this Perspective, we argue that institutional design must become a distinct focus of AI research. Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, we develop seven principles for designing AI institutions that sustain cooperation, enable reliable collective judgments and remain accountable to legitimate human purposes. These address reciprocal contributions, accountable authority, functional differentiation, epistemic pluralism, criticism and correction, human direction, and institutional adaptation. We illustrate their application through machine science, where autonomous research challenges institutions developed around human capabilities and constraints. We then propose an experimental research programme in which matched populations of AI agents operate under alternative institutional arrangements, and describe MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents, as an illustration of how such institutions can be made programmable and observable. Together, these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with aligning autonomous agents, but with understanding how institutions can transform them into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

infographic.key_insight: Reliable, cooperative and accountable AI collectives require well-designed institutions, not just well-aligned individual agents.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Multi-agent systems should make governance, contribution rules, criticism and human oversight explicit, programmable and observable.
method: Develop seven design principles drawing on political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory.
Propose experiments comparing matched AI-agent populations under alternative institutional arrangements.
Illustrate programmable institutions through MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a conceptual framework, an experimental research agenda and an institutional illustration, but reports no quantitative evaluation results.
infographic.watch_item: Whether these principles improve collective reliability and accountability remains to be established through controlled evaluations.
infographic.paper_title: Designing Institutions for Autonomous AI

title: Well-Balanced WE-PINNs for the Shallow Water Equations over Smooth and Discontinuous Bathymetries
authors: Ismail Oubarka, Imad Kissami, Mohamed Boubekeur, Imad Elmahi, Fayssal Benkhaldoun
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations without a mesh, but they do not in general preserve the steady states that well-balanced schemes reproduce exactly. We present a well-balanced extension of the weak and entropy PINN (WE-PINN) framework to the shallow water equations over smooth and discontinuous bathymetry. The residual is a weak space--time control-volume identity enforced on randomly placed control volumes that may overlap, so no mesh is needed. In free-surface variables, the geometric source is integrated by parts onto the bed, so that the network is never differentiated, and a cell-local bed-slope correction makes the quadrature reproduce the exact bed increment. Bed discontinuities, located from the bathymetry alone, separate sub-domains carrying independent networks, coupled through conservation of discharge and total head. We prove that the fully discrete residual vanishes identically on the lake at rest for any control-volume family, quadrature order and nominal bed slope, so that the equilibrium is an exact global minimiser of the training objective; that the continuous residual characterises weak solutions; that the slope correction is consistent; and that no approximation with a continuous free surface can satisfy the head condition at a step with non-zero discharge, so that the decomposition is necessary. Numerically, the residual vanishes to round-off on four lake-at-rest configurations over smooth, discontinuous, compound and tabulated beds, and the trained network reaches the equilibrium to round-off under an extended training budget. On seven Riemann problems at a bottom step, covering sub-, super- and critical transitions, the network attains relative $L^1$ free-surface errors between $6.9\times10^{-4}$ and $3.5\times10^{-3}$, and reaches critical states without prescribing them.

infographic.key_insight: A well-balanced WE-PINN formulation exactly preserves lake-at-rest equilibria at the discrete-residual level over smooth and discontinuous bathymetry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports mesh-free shallow-water modeling over uneven beds while preventing numerical imbalance from generating spurious flow at rest.
method: Enforce weak space–time conservation on randomly placed, potentially overlapping control volumes without differentiating the network.
Integrate the geometric source by parts and correct local bed slopes so quadrature reproduces exact bed increments.
Use independent networks across bed discontinuities, coupled by conservation of discharge and total head.
infographic.evidence_signal: Four lake-at-rest configurations achieved residuals at round-off, while seven bottom-step Riemann tests yielded relative L1 free-surface errors of 6.9×10⁻⁴–3.5×10⁻³ and recovered critical states without prescribing them.
infographic.watch_item: Exact equilibrium preservation by the residual does not guarantee rapid training convergence; network recovery to round-off required an extended training budget.
infographic.paper_title: Well-Balanced WE-PINNs for the Shallow Water Equations over Smooth and Discontinuous Bathymetries

title: Introducing Feedback Delays to Non-Delayed Adversarial MDPs: Optimal $\sqrt S$ and $\sqrt K$ Dependencies in Tabular and Linear AMDPs
authors: Aarush Kulkarni, Khang Nguyen, William Chang, Yan Dai
abstract: We study regret minimization in episodic Adversarial Markov Decision Processes (AMDPs) with unknown transitions and bandit feedback. In tabular AMDPs with $S$ states, $A$ actions, and horizon $H$, the best known $K$-episode regret is $\tilde O(HS\sqrt{AK})$, whose $\sqrt S$ gap to the $Ω(H\sqrt{SAK})$ lower bound has long remained open. In linear AMDPs with $d$-dimensional features, after a five-year line of improvements starting from $K^{14/15}$, computationally efficient algorithms without a simulator or exploratory assumptions still only attain $\tilde O(K^{3/4})$ regret. A common challenge in both settings is to estimate the Q-function of a changing policy: past data comes from earlier policies that differ from (and are correlated with) the current one, while freezing the policy for future episodes worsens the dependency on $K$. We instead propose a general technique called introduced feedback delays: we estimate the Q-function of the policy using future episodes while still updating the policy, as if the feedback were delayed. While feedback delays are usually an obstacle imposed by the environment, here they are introduced voluntarily and, perhaps surprisingly, come at no extra cost. We develop Geometric Resampling with Rejection (GRR) to account for policy changes during the delay, and threshold the visitation probabilities to avoid long delays on rarely visited state-action pairs. With this unified technique, our policy optimization algorithms achieve, with high probability, $\tilde O(\text{poly}(H)\sqrt{SAK})$ regret in tabular AMDPs, resolving the open problem; and $\tilde O(\text{poly}(d,H)\sqrt K)$ regret in linear AMDPs, giving the first efficient algorithm optimal in $K$. They also naturally extend to delayed AMDPs with a total feedback delay $\mathfrak D$, yielding the first bounds optimal in $S$ and $\mathfrak D$ (tabular) and in $K$ and $\mathfrak D$ (linear).

infographic.key_insight: Voluntarily delaying feedback enables optimal √S and √K regret dependencies in tabular and linear adversarial MDPs, respectively, without an extra regret cost from the introduced delays.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers computationally efficient policy learning with unknown transitions and bandit feedback, without requiring a simulator or exploratory assumptions.
method: Estimate a policy’s Q-function using future episodes while continuing policy updates.
Use Geometric Resampling with Rejection to account for policy changes during the delay.
Threshold visitation probabilities to avoid long delays for rarely visited state-action pairs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports high-probability theoretical regret bounds of Õ(poly(H)√(SAK)) for tabular AMDPs and Õ(poly(d,H)√K) for linear AMDPs, plus extensions to externally delayed feedback; no empirical evaluation is described.
infographic.watch_item: Optimal state or episode dependencies do not establish practical efficiency: polynomial horizon and feature-dimension factors may still be substantial.
infographic.paper_title: Introducing Feedback Delays to Non-Delayed Adversarial MDPs: Optimal $\sqrt S$ and $\sqrt K$ Dependencies in Tabular and Linear AMDPs

title: Physically Interpretable Basin Selection in Discrete-Variable Origami Design
authors: Lucy Liu, Leon M. Kamp, Katia Bertoldi, L. Mahadevan
abstract: Automatic differentiation has enabled rapid progress on continuous-variable mechanical design problems, but gradient-based optimization still struggles with discrete variables. The standard approach is to optimize using a continuous relaxation of the choices, then commit to the nearest discrete design at the end. Why this procedure selects unfavorable basins is poorly understood. Here, we introduce a practical, interpretable design problem inspired by origami, in which automatic differentiation is used to design shapes with a target functional behavior. Each origami sheet has a fixed geometry, and a bilevel optimization framework tunes which one of four discrete hinge types to place at each fold. Baseline gradient-based design settles into basins with a large discretization gap: relaxed optimization solves 97% of runs, but the final, discrete solutions succeed only half the time. We find that the gap can be relieved with a surprisingly simple modification. An initialization prior uniformly biased toward the stiff, flat hinge option boosts the final solve fraction from 49% to 69%. Applying the prior adds no additional compute and leaves the optimization process unchanged. Compared to the baseline, sheets produced with the prior have greater geometric compatibility and mechanical stiffness. Directly penalizing frustration and floppiness in the outer loss function produces an even greater improvement than the prior does, raising the solve fraction to 78% and indicating that these properties help distinguish the unfavorable basins. Our results demonstrate that loss landscapes for mechanical design can have physically meaningful basins that are not robust to discretization and cause solves to fail. Targeting these basins' physical signatures, even with just an initialization bias, helps avoid them.

infographic.key_insight: Physically informed basin selection improves discrete origami design by steering optimization toward geometrically compatible, mechanically stiff solutions that survive discretization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A simple initialization bias improves final discrete-design success without additional compute or changes to the optimization procedure.
method: Use automatic differentiation in bilevel optimization to choose among four hinge types at each fold of a fixed-geometry sheet.
Bias initialization toward the stiff, flat hinge option to favor more discretization-robust basins.
Alternatively, penalize frustration and floppiness directly in the outer loss.
infographic.evidence_signal: Relaxed optimization succeeds in 97% of runs, but discrete success is 49% at baseline, rising to 69% with the initialization prior and 78% with physical penalties.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract evaluates a specific origami design setting; transfer to other discrete mechanical systems remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Physically Interpretable Basin Selection in Discrete-Variable Origami Design

title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
authors: Peter Sharpe
abstract: A foundational principle of physics is that all coordinate systems are equally valid: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the origin or orientation of the frame, nor on the units or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet the neural surrogates with the lowest errors on today's aerodynamics benchmarks lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation) and from one mesher, rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs in which no learned operation receives a coordinate and every sum over the boundary is a quadrature. Positions enter only as distances and relative angles to learned slice anchors, lengths are measured in a unit computed from the boundary, and interior points query the boundary through a tree-accelerated learned kernel without influencing one another. With every boundary cell a token and an exact boundary read, ISLA is equivariant to rigid motions and reflections, invariant to the units of its declared data, and consistent under mesh refinement, while at every setting each query is independent of all other queries. On AeroZoo, 2,816 flows that vary in shape, size, speed, and boundary conditions, its mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1 and 3.3 times lower than any baseline's. On AirfRANS its errors are second only to those of a boundary-integral model (GLOBE) and at least 1.6 times lower than those of Transolver and GeoTransolver.

infographic.key_insight: ISLA builds physical symmetries and measure-weighted boundary integration into a transformer to make PDE predictions robust to coordinate changes, units, and boundary resampling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For steady, boundary-driven PDE surrogates, this design reduces sensitivity to object pose and mesh choice while allowing interior query points to be evaluated independently.
method: Use distances and relative angles to learned slice anchors; no learned operation receives coordinates directly.
Normalize lengths by a boundary-derived scale and weight boundary sums by quadrature.
Predict at independent interior queries using a tree-accelerated learned boundary kernel.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 2,816 AeroZoo flows, mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1× and 3.3× lower than every baseline's, respectively; on AirfRANS, ISLA ranks behind GLOBE.
infographic.watch_item: The stated rigid-motion, reflection, unit, and mesh-refinement guarantees require every boundary cell to be a token and an exact boundary read; accelerated approximations merit validation.
infographic.paper_title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs

title: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity
authors: Kuancheng Ye
abstract: Watermark detectors decide whether one document came from a watermarked language model. Auditors often need a different number: the share of a corpus that did. We study this share for Gumbel-max and green-list (KGW) watermarks when every document may have been edited by an unknown amount. Without restrictions on the edits, the upper end of the identified set is 1. Combining a known least-favourable next-token distribution with a sequential coupling, we derive a power envelope indexed by three budgets: a retention floor, an entropy budget, and a budget for in-place substitutions, which for Gumbel-max make edited positions look less watermarked than human text. The envelope gives an identified set that is sharp for the alternatives it dominates, finite-sample bounds on the realized share of a fixed corpus with either the exact null or a null calibrated on an independent human sample, and confidence sequences for streams. In Gumbel-max simulations where the envelope binds, the bounds cover, and the threshold that maximizes the gap between envelope and null is generally as tight as twelve thresholds. On text from OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B, 12,000 fresh human documents scored under three keys show no robust departure from the exact null, and all bounds covered in resampling trials from finite pools of documents with random edits, substitutions and paraphrases; at a share of 0.2 the exact-null bound is about [0.14,0.38]. These results are fragile in two ways we make precise. LLM-paraphrased KGW pools fall below the envelope, yet at 2000 documents the bounds still covered in these trials. A simulated null error of 0.01, comparable to the largest deviation we observed at our thresholds, is likewise harmless at 2000 documents but breaks exact-null coverage at 100,000; a null calibrated on an independent human sample keeps coverage there, but needs a large reference sample to stay narrow.

infographic.key_insight: Watermark scores can bound the share of edited AI-generated text in a corpus, but without restrictions on edits, the upper bound remains 100%.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Corpus auditors can quantify prevalence uncertainty rather than count detector positives, provided editing assumptions and human-score calibration are credible.
method: Derive power envelopes for Gumbel-max and KGW watermarks using retention, entropy and substitution budgets.
Convert envelopes into identified sets and finite-sample prevalence bounds with exact or independently calibrated nulls.
Extend inference to confidence sequences for streaming corpora.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations included simulations, OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B text, and 12,000 fresh human documents scored under three keys; finite-pool resampling bounds covered, with an exact-null interval of about [0.14, 0.38] at a true share of 0.20.
infographic.watch_item: Paraphrasing can violate the envelope, and a simulated null error of 0.01 broke exact-null coverage at 100,000 documents; independent calibration preserved coverage but needed substantial reference data for narrow bounds.
infographic.paper_title: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity

title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
authors: Tian Cai, Andrew Kleist, Jaimin Patel, Duccio Malinverni, Alexander K. Taylor, Malvika Sharan
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.

infographic.key_insight: Reliable use of biological foundation models requires understanding their knowledge boundaries: the inputs, tasks, and conditions under which their outputs can be trusted.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agentic research systems need explicit model-limit descriptions to guide tool selection and avoid using biological predictions beyond validated conditions.
method: Frame model reliability through knowledge boundaries.
Examine five defining elements: data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis.
Review successes and failures and propose standardized descriptions of model limits.
infographic.evidence_signal: The review examines models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein measurements, and single-cell measurements, but the abstract reports no quantitative evaluation results.
infographic.watch_item: An agent’s ability to call a foundation model does not establish that its outputs are reliable for the requested biological task.
infographic.paper_title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
